resources.string: Never close this one on me
You\'ve opened %1$s a few times just now.
What are you here to do in %1$s?
Pick a time box — you\'ll get a gentle nudge when it\'s up.
Chosen apps stop interrupting you; their notifications wait quietly and arrive together at 8:00, 12:30 and 18:00. Conversations, calls and alarms always come through instantly.
Grant notification access to enable batching
One calm summary per batch of held notifications.
Nothing here. When batching is on, held notifications collect in this journal so nothing is ever lost.
A quiet landscape under the sky. Even a brief glance at greenery or water measurably steadies attention, so this is drawn to be looked at — and never to move.

If you write down a few small things that help you, one of them is offered — beside the app, never instead of it — at the moment you reach for something else. Only your words, never ours. Nothing is offered on a fourth reach in ten minutes, or during your quiet hours: those are not moments to be asked whether you have tried going for a walk.
Anything still open? Put it down here and pick it up in the morning.
The one thing on your mind
You left this for yourself last night:

These are ones you have gone through every time. That might mean the pause has become scenery, or it might mean it is quietly doing its job and you genuinely wanted to go in. Only you know which. Nothing changes unless you change it.
%1$s — shown %2$d times, and you went in every time.
You have not named anything yet. You do not have to.

On its own, the pause only appears when you open an app from this screen. Tapping a notification, swiping through recents or following a link goes straight in — which is most of how a phone actually gets used. Turning this on means the pause applies however you arrive.

Android calls this an accessibility service, and that sounds worse than it is. It is set up so it cannot read your screen — not messages, not passwords, not what you are looking at. It is told the name of the app that came to the front, and nothing else. Android enforces that, not us.
On. The pause applies however you open an app.
Off. The pause only applies from this screen.
Lets the pause apply when you open an app from a notification or from recents, not just from the home screen.

MindAnchor uses this to notice when an app you have chosen a pause for comes to the front, so the pause works however you opened it. It cannot read your screen — only the name of the app that arrived.

Through your quiet hours the phone goes priority-only: starred contacts and repeat callers still reach you, everything else waits for morning. Set the hours to your night, not to a default — shift work and being on call are the norm, not the exception.
Grant Do Not Disturb access to enable sunset
Wind down through the quiet hours
MindAnchor can estimate your sleep window from when the screen goes quiet at night — on this phone only, no wearable, nothing uploaded. Consistency matters more than hours.
Grant usage access to see your rhythm
Not enough nights recorded yet. Check back in a few days.
This is an estimate of how consistent your nightly phone-quiet window is — regular timing, not total hours, is what the research links to better mood and sleep.
Set MindAnchor as your home screen
Nothing hidden. Long-press any app to hide it from the drawer — it stays reachable by typing its exact name.
A calmer phone, built from published research. No accounts, no server — everything stays on this device. You choose what turns on; nothing is imposed.
What pulls at you? Pick what fits.
Apps I open without meaning to
My phone keeps me up at night
I want to know if any of this helps
Your plan — switch each on when ready:
• Notification batching (settings): chosen apps go quiet and arrive together three times a day. People always come through.
• Long-press any app and choose \"Add a pause\" — a breath and an intention before it opens.
• Sunset mode + sleep rhythm (settings): priority-only nights and a view of how regular your sleep is.
• The wellbeing pulse (settings): a 2-minute check-in every two weeks, scored honestly.
Explore at your own pace — every feature lives in settings and long-press menus, all off by default.
A 2-minute WHO-5 check-in every two weeks. It\'s how you — and MindAnchor — know honestly whether any of this is helping.
How have the last two weeks felt?
Five statements, answered 0 (at no time) to 5 (all of the time). This is a self-check, not a diagnosis.
0 = at no time · 5 = all of the time
Scores in this range are common when things are heavy. Your people and your plan are one tap from the home screen whenever you want them.
Two weeks since your last pulse
Somewhere to write down what helps, and the people you would want to talk to. Yours to fill in, whenever you feel like it.
Everything here works offline and stays on this phone. It reaches real people — it never tries to be one.
No one added yet. You can add the people you\'d actually call, below.
MindAnchor is a wellness tool, not a treatment, and not a medical device. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

Three skills from dialectical behaviour therapy, the treatment with the strongest evidence for getting through emotional crises. They are for riding out the next few minutes — nothing more is being asked of you.
Stop. Take a step back. Observe what is happening, inside and around you. Proceed mindfully — pick the next small action, not the whole day.

Cold water on your face or hands. Intense movement for a minute. Paced breathing, out longer than in. Then relax each muscle group in turn. These change body chemistry fast when thinking alone will not.

The cold water and the hard movement both swing your heart rate on purpose. If you have a heart condition, an eating disorder, or are pregnant, skip those two and ask a doctor first. The paced breathing and the muscle relaxation are gentle, and they work on their own.
Name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, one you can taste. Slowly, out loud if you can.
Nothing written yet. A plan is easiest to write on a calm day, for a day that is not — that is the whole idea.
Thoughts, feelings or situations I notice first
What helps me on my own
Things I can do without anyone else
Where I can go, who I can be around
Places and people that take the edge off
What I want to stay for
What I can put away, and who can hold it
A number is what makes this callable. Add one to save this person.
These people are never batched and never held back by sunset mode — if they reach out, your phone tells you straight away.
This phone could not open a dialer. The number is %1$s — call it from your phone app, or ask someone near you to.

Everything else here can be walked through, which is usually right and useless on the nights it matters. If this phone is set up as its own guardian, the apps you chose a pause for become genuinely unopenable through the quiet hours — a decision made while calm, kept by the phone rather than by you.
This has to be granted once from a computer, on a phone with no accounts signed in — usually right after a factory reset. It is a high bar on purpose.
This phone is set up as its own guardian. Chosen apps close for the quiet hours.
Your phone app, messages, settings and this app are never suspended, whatever you choose.
Any suspended apps open again straight away. Getting this back later needs another factory reset, so it is worth being sure — but if you want it back, take it back.

A grey screen is the single most effective change measured in this field — not through willpower, but because colour is most of what makes a feed feel alive. Trials consistently find people put the phone down sooner without it.
Android will not let an app turn this on by itself, which is the right rule. Run this once from a computer with the phone plugged in, and it sticks through reboots:
Go grey through the quiet hours

This borrows Android\'s colour correction, so the two cannot both be on at once. Whatever correction you had set is put back when the grey screen goes off. If you rely on it during the day, you may still want to leave the night setting alone.
Nothing here is backed up to the cloud, on purpose — so a reset or lost phone would take your plan and your people with it. Save a copy somewhere you trust, and bring it back whenever you need to.
Saved. Keep it somewhere only you can reach.
That file isn\'t a MindAnchor copy, or it came from a newer version. Nothing was changed.
Couldn\'t read or write that file. Nothing was changed.

MindAnchor is an open-source, research-backed launcher. It has no accounts, no server and no analytics — your data never leaves this phone. It is a wellness tool, not a medical device, and it is no substitute for talking to someone.
